items.prompt: What is the null hypothesis in a hypothesis test?

options.label: The claim that the sample is perfectly random
The claim that the p-value will be below 0.05
The claim that there is no effect or no difference
The claim that the researcher hopes the data will support

rubric: The null hypothesis is the default claim of no effect or no difference.
Distractors confuse it with the alternative hypothesis the researcher hopes to support.

items.prompt: Which describes a p-value?

options.label: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true, given the observed sample data
The probability of data at least this extreme if the null is true
The chance that the same test result will replicate if the study is run again
The probability that the null hypothesis is true, given the observed sample data

rubric: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true and measures how extreme the data are.
Distractors treat it as the probability of a hypothesis, a common misreading.

items.prompt: What is a Type I error?

options.label: Using the wrong test for the data type
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true
Collecting a sample that is too small to analyse
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is false

rubric: Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a true null.
Option 0 describes a Type II error, the most common mix-up.

items.prompt: Which significance level (alpha) is most commonly used as the default cut-off in hypothesis testing?

options.label: 0.50 divided by n

rubric: 0.05 is the conventional default alpha.
0.95 is confused with the confidence level.

items.prompt: Which test is designed to compare the means of two independent groups?

options.label: Shapiro-Wilk test
Chi-square test
One-proportion z-test
Two-sample t-test

rubric: The two-sample t-test compares two group means.
Chi-square is for counts of categories, not means.

items.prompt: Which of these are specified when setting up a hypothesis test? Select all that apply.

options.label: A significance level alpha
The prior probability that the null is true
A null hypothesis
An alternative hypothesis
A guarantee that results will replicate

rubric: A test needs a null, an alternative and an alpha chosen beforehand.
Prior probabilities belong to Bayesian methods, and replication cannot be guaranteed.

items.prompt: A website team states: "H0: the new checkout button does not change the conversion rate." They plan to test whether the new button changes conversion in either direction. Which is the matching alternative hypothesis, H1?

options.label: The new button does not lower the conversion rate
The conversion rate is exactly the same for both buttons
The new button raises conversion by at least 10%
The conversion rate differs between the two buttons

rubric: A two-sided H1 states the rate differs, matching the plan to detect change in either direction.
Other options are the null, a specific effect size, or a one-sided claim.

items.prompt: A test gives p = 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.label: The observed effect is about 3% of the size of one standard deviation
Given the data we saw, there is only a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true
If the null were true, data this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
Given the data we saw, there is a 97% chance that the alternative hypothesis is true

rubric: The p-value is a probability of the data given the null, not of the null.
Options 0 and 1 are the classic misreading as a probability of a hypothesis.

items.prompt: A study fails to reject the null hypothesis (p = 0.20). What can be concluded?

options.label: The null hypothesis has been proven true by the data
The sample must have been collected incorrectly or was too small
The alternative hypothesis has been proven false by the test
The data gave too little evidence against the null

rubric: Failing to reject means insufficient evidence, not proof of the null.
Options 0 and 2 treat absence of evidence as proof.

items.prompt: A researcher lowers alpha from 0.05 to 0.01, keeping everything else the same. What is the expected effect?

options.label: Fewer Type II errors and fewer Type I errors
More Type I errors but fewer Type II errors
Fewer Type I errors but more Type II errors
No change, since alpha only affects reporting

rubric: A stricter alpha makes rejection harder, trading false positives for false negatives.
Option 1 ignores the trade-off between the two error types.

items.prompt: Why does increasing the sample size generally make a test better at detecting a real effect?

options.label: It reduces the standard error, so real differences stand out more
It guarantees the p-value will fall below alpha, even if no effect exists
It makes the null hypothesis more likely to be true, so tests are more precise
It raises alpha automatically, so rejecting the null becomes easier

rubric: Larger samples shrink the standard error and raise power.
Option 1 overstates: it does not guarantee significance when there is no effect.

items.prompt: A survey records, for 200 people, their favourite of three drink brands and whether they are under or over 30. Which test suits checking whether brand preference is associated with age group?

options.label: Chi-square test of independence on the counts
Two-sample t-test comparing mean age across the brands
One-sample t-test on how often each brand is chosen
Paired t-test on each person's brand and age group

rubric: Both variables are categorical, so counts in a table suit a chi-square test of independence.
The t-tests need numeric measurements to compare means.

items.prompt: Which statements about statistical significance are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A significant result can still reflect a tiny, unimportant effect
A p-value below alpha means the data would be unusual if the null were true
A significant result means the alternative is certainly true
A non-significant result shows there is no effect at all

rubric: Significance reflects evidence against the null, not effect size or certainty.
Non-significance is not proof of no effect, and significance is not certainty.

items.prompt: An A/B test on 2 million visitors finds the new page raises conversion from 5.00% to 5.05% with p = 0.04, using alpha = 0.05. A colleague says the new page is clearly a big improvement. How should the result be interpreted?

options.label: With a sample this large the p-value is unreliable, so no conclusion can be drawn about the page
The result is not significant because the difference is under 1%, so the page has no effect
The difference is significant but may be too small to matter
The p-value shows a 96% chance that the new page is a big improvement over the old one

rubric: With very large samples, tiny effects can be statistically significant yet practically small.
Option 1 misreads the p-value as a probability about the hypothesis.

items.prompt: A test of a new drug against a placebo gives p = 0.03. Which interpretation of this p-value is correct?

options.label: The drug's true effect is about 3% of the size of the observed difference
There is a 97% chance that the drug works, given the data we observed in this trial
If the drug had no effect, results this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
Given the data we observed, there is only a 3% chance that the drug has no real effect at all

rubric: A p-value is the probability of data this extreme assuming the null hypothesis is true.
The distractors treat it as the probability that the null or alternative hypothesis is true, which is a common misreading.

items.prompt: In hypothesis testing, what is a Type I error?

options.label: Choosing a test that does not match the data type
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true
Using a sample too small to estimate the mean
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false

rubric: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis, with probability alpha.
The second option describes a Type II error, which learners often swap with Type I.

items.prompt: A team wants to test whether a redesigned checkout page changes the conversion rate. Which null hypothesis is stated correctly?

options.label: The new page has a higher conversion rate than the old page
The new page's conversion rate is exactly 100%
The conversion rates for the old and new pages differ
The conversion rate is the same for the old and new pages

rubric: The null hypothesis states no difference or no effect.
The distractors are alternative hypotheses (one-sided or two-sided), which learners often mistake for the null.

items.prompt: For which situation is a chi-square test of independence the appropriate kind of test?

options.label: Checking whether device type (phone, laptop, tablet) is linked to subscribing (yes or no)
Comparing the same patients' weights measured before and after a 12-week diet program
Comparing the average heights of two independent groups of students from different schools
Checking whether two continuous measurements, such as height and weight, rise and fall together

rubric: Chi-square tests of independence compare two categorical variables using counts.
The other options describe a two-sample t-test, correlation and a paired t-test, which fit numeric data.

items.prompt: An analyst lowers the significance level from 0.05 to 0.01 without changing the sample size. What is the most likely effect?

options.label: Type I error risk rises, because a stricter test rejects the null more readily
Neither error risk changes, since sample size is fixed
Type I error risk falls, but Type II error risk tends to rise
Both Type I and Type II error risks fall, because the test is more rigorous

rubric: A stricter alpha makes false positives rarer but makes it harder to detect real effects, so Type II risk rises.
Learners often think a stricter threshold reduces every kind of error.

items.prompt: A study returns p = 0.20 at alpha = 0.05, so the analyst fails to reject the null hypothesis. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: The result shows the alternative hypothesis is false
A small sample may have left the test without power to detect a real effect
The probability that the null hypothesis is true is 20%
The result shows that there is no effect at all
The data do not prove that the null hypothesis is true

rubric: Failing to reject means the evidence was insufficient, not that the null is proven; low power is a common reason.
Distractors treat absence of evidence as evidence of absence, or read p as the probability of the null.

items.prompt: A company tests a new app layout on 2 million users. The conversion rate rises from 5.00% to 5.05%, with p = 0.04. A manager says the redesign is clearly a big success because the result is significant. What is the best interpretation of the result?

options.label: The difference is statistically significant, but it is tiny and may be too small to matter in practice
The difference is proven real, because a sample of 2 million users removes all chance of error
The difference is large, because a p-value below 0.05 indicates a big effect on conversion
The difference is probably due to chance, because the observed gain is only 0.05 points

rubric: With very large samples, tiny effects can be significant; significance does not measure effect size.
Distractors equate small p with large effect, or dismiss a significant result, or claim certainty.

items.prompt: A sample of n = 25 has mean 52 and standard deviation 10. Test H0: mean = 50 with a one-sample t-test. What is the t statistic?
rubric: Distractors come from forgetting to divide by sqrt(n) or using n instead of its square root.

items.prompt: Before collecting data, a team specified a one-sided test (H1: new method is faster) at alpha = 0.05. The software reports a two-sided p = 0.08, and the observed difference is in the predicted direction. What is the decision?

options.label: Fail to reject H0, since 0.08 is above 0.05
Reject H0, since 0.08 is below 0.10
Fail to reject H0, since the one-sided p-value is 0.16
Reject H0, since the one-sided p-value is 0.04

rubric: For a one-sided test in the predicted direction, the p-value is half the two-sided value: 0.04 < 0.05.
Distractors ignore the one-sided halving or double instead of halving.

items.prompt: In a 2x2 table of 200 people, one row total is 80 and one column total is 50. Under independence, what is the expected count in the cell where that row and column meet?
rubric: Expected count = row total x column total / grand total = 80 x 50 / 200 = 20.
Distractors come from using the wrong totals or dividing by the wrong number.

items.prompt: A chi-square test of independence is run on a table with 3 rows and 4 columns. How many degrees of freedom does it have?
rubric: df = (rows - 1) x (columns - 1) = 2 x 3 = 6.
Distractors use the number of cells, or rows + columns - 1 or -2, instead of the product.

items.prompt: Blood pressure is measured for the same 30 patients before and after a treatment. Which test best fits the question of whether the mean blood pressure changed?

options.label: Two-sample t-test treating the groups as independent
One-sample t-test on the pooled 60 readings
Paired t-test on the 30 differences
Chi-square test of independence on the counts

rubric: Measurements on the same patients are paired, so test the mean of the within-patient differences.
Treating paired data as two independent samples ignores the pairing.

items.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for the difference in mean scores between two groups is (-0.5, 3.5). Apply this to a two-sided test of H0: difference = 0 at alpha = 0.05. Which conclusions follow? Select all that apply.

options.label: The test would reject H0, because the interval is fairly narrow
There is a 95% probability that the true difference lies in this interval
The p-value would be above 0.05
The test would reject H0, because most of the interval is positive
The test would fail to reject H0, because 0 lies inside the interval

rubric: A 95% interval containing 0 corresponds to p > 0.05 in a two-sided test at alpha = 0.05.
Distractors judge by where most of the interval lies, or by width, or misstate what the confidence level means.

items.prompt: A marketer runs 10 separate A/B tests, each at alpha = 0.05, and tests 9 of them show nothing. One test gives p = 0.03 and is reported as a winner. The team decides to apply a Bonferroni correction across all 10 tests. What should they conclude?

options.label: The corrected threshold is 0.05, so p = 0.03 is significant
The corrected threshold is 0.5, so p = 0.03 is significant
The corrected threshold is 0.0005, so p = 0.03 is not significant
The corrected threshold is 0.005, so p = 0.03 is not significant

rubric: Bonferroni divides alpha by the number of tests: 0.05 / 10 = 0.005, and 0.03 exceeds it.
Distractors multiply instead of divide, skip the correction, or miscompute the threshold.

items.prompt: A sample of 25 observations has mean 52 and standard deviation 10. You test H0: mu = 50 with a one-sample t-test. What is the t statistic?
rubric: Using 10 instead of the standard error (giving 0.2) or forgetting to divide by sqrt(n) (giving 2.0) are the common slips.

items.prompt: The same 30 patients have their blood pressure measured before and after a drug. You want to test H0: no mean change. Which test fits?

options.label: Chi-square test of independence on before and after readings
Paired t-test on the 30 within-patient differences
One-sample z-test on the after readings against a mean of zero
Two-sample t-test treating before and after as independent groups

rubric: Measurements on the same patients are dependent, so a paired t-test on differences is appropriate.
The independent two-sample test ignores the pairing, a common misconception.

items.prompt: A one-sided test with a symmetric test statistic gives p = 0.03 in the observed direction. You must instead report a two-sided test at alpha = 0.05. What is the correct result?

options.label: p = 0.03, so reject H0
p = 0.015, so reject H0
p = 0.97, so fail to reject H0
p = 0.06, so fail to reject H0

rubric: For a symmetric statistic the two-sided p-value doubles the one-sided one: 0.06 > 0.05, so fail to reject.
Halving the p-value or keeping it unchanged confuses one-sided and two-sided tests.

items.prompt: In a contingency table of 200 people, a cell's row total is 80 and its column total is 50. Under independence, what is the expected count for that cell?
rubric: Expected = row total x column total / grand total = 80 x 50 / 200 = 20.
Other options come from mis-dividing or forgetting to divide by the grand total.

items.prompt: You run a chi-square test of independence on a contingency table with 3 rows and 4 columns. How many degrees of freedom does the test have?
rubric: df = (rows - 1)(columns - 1) = 2 x 3 = 6.
Using rc or rc - 1 confuses this with goodness-of-fit df.

items.prompt: A test returns p = 0.03 with alpha set at 0.05 beforehand. Which statements correctly apply this result? Select all that apply.

options.label: The result would not be significant if alpha had been set at 0.01
If H0 were true, results at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
The effect must be large, because p is well below 0.05 and so the result is practically important
There is a 3% probability that H0 is true
H0 is rejected at the 5% level

rubric: p < 0.05 means reject at 5%, p is the probability of data this extreme given H0, and 0.03 > 0.01 so it fails at 1%.
The 3% chance that H0 is true is the classic misreading of the p-value.

items.prompt: An A/B test shows 200 conversions out of 2000 visitors for page A and 250 out of 2000 for page B. You run a two-proportion z-test of H0: pA = pB. Which proportion goes into the standard error formula under H0?

options.label: The page A proportion 200/2000 = 0.10
The pooled proportion 450/4000 = 0.1125
The difference between proportions, 0.025
The page B proportion 250/2000 = 0.125

rubric: Under H0 both pages share one proportion, so the pooled estimate 0.1125 is used for the SE.
Using one group's proportion or the difference ignores the null assumption.

items.prompt: A researcher tests 20 unrelated outcomes, each at alpha = 0.05 and with no real effects. One outcome gives p = 0.03 and is reported as a discovery. What is the main flaw?

options.label: A two-sided alternative splits alpha across both tails, which doubles the false-positive rate for this one outcome
With 20 tests, at least one false positive is likely (about 64%), so no correction was applied
A very large sample makes every p-value small, so p = 0.03 only reflects the sample size and not a real effect
A p-value of 0.03 is too close to the 0.05 cutoff to be trusted, so only p-values below 0.01 count as evidence

rubric: The chance of at least one false positive across 20 independent tests is 1 - 0.95^20, about 64%, so a correction such as Bonferroni is needed.
Blaming the closeness to 0.05 or sidedness misses the multiplicity problem.

items.prompt: Students measured the same 25 runners before and after a training programme, then used an independent two-sample t-test and found p = 0.20. A paired t-test gives p = 0.01. What best explains the gap?

options.label: The independent test counts 50 separate observations instead of 25 pairs, so it overstates the evidence and inflates the effect
The paired test assumes equal group sizes and equal variances, which makes it a less strict test than the independent one
The paired test uses fewer degrees of freedom than the independent test, and fewer degrees of freedom always lower p
Between-runner variability inflates the standard error in the independent test; pairing removes it

rubric: Runners differ a lot from each other; pairing removes that variance, shrinking the SE and raising power.
Fewer df actually lowers power slightly, so that distractor reverses the logic.

items.prompt: A study with 2,000,000 users finds a mean difference of 0.1 points on a 100-point satisfaction scale with p < 0.001. A manager concludes the change is important. What is the best analysis?

options.label: The p-value is far below 0.001, so the effect must be large and the manager is right to call it important
With such a large n, even a trivial difference gives a tiny p-value, so judge effect size separately
The huge sample means the test almost certainly violated its assumptions, so the p-value cannot be trusted at all
A p-value below 0.001 means the null hypothesis has been proven false, so the effect is real and meaningful

rubric: Standard error shrinks with n, so trivial effects become significant; practical importance needs effect size or a confidence interval.
The p-value does not measure effect size.

items.prompt: A chi-square test on a 3x3 table has several cells with expected counts below 2 and gives p = 0.04. Why is this result questionable?

options.label: Small expected counts bias the test toward failing to reject, so p = 0.04 understates how significant the result really is
Chi-square cannot be applied to tables bigger than 2x2 unless a continuity correction is applied to every cell first
Small expected counts make the chi-square approximation unreliable, so exact methods or merged categories are needed
Chi-square is only valid when every observed count exceeds 100, so a table with smaller counts cannot be tested

rubric: The test statistic follows a chi-square distribution only approximately, and poorly when expected counts are small.
The rules concern expected counts, not observed counts or table size.

items.prompt: An analyst checks an A/B test every day and stops the first time p < 0.05. The true effect is zero. Why does this procedure produce more than 5% false positives?

options.label: Each daily check uses a smaller sample than the planned one, so the test becomes too strict and the p-values are unreliable
The p-value tends to shrink as data accumulate even with no real effect, so it eventually falls below 0.05 by default
Repeated looks give many chances for chance fluctuation to cross 0.05, inflating overall Type I error
Stopping early biases the estimated standard deviation downward, which makes every test statistic too large

rubric: Each look is another test; the chance that at least one crosses 0.05 grows with the number of looks.
Distractors invent mechanical effects on p-values or variance.

items.prompt: For a two-sample t-test, which changes would, all else equal, increase the power to detect a true difference? Select all that apply.

options.label: Lowering alpha from 0.05 to 0.01
Raising alpha from 0.01 to 0.05
Using groups drawn from a more variable population
Collecting a larger sample in each group
Reducing measurement noise so the standard deviation is smaller

rubric: Larger n, smaller variance and a more lenient alpha all raise power, though the last also raises Type I error.
Lowering alpha or increasing variability reduces power.

items.prompt: A trial of a tutoring programme reports a mean score gain of 2.0 points, with a 95% CI for the difference of (-0.5, 4.5) and p = 0.11. A colleague says, "The test proves tutoring has no effect." What is the best analysis?

options.label: The colleague is right, because the interval is centred on a positive value but still includes zero, so any gain is due to chance
The colleague is right, because p exceeds 0.05, which shows the true difference is exactly zero and not just small
The result is significant, because most of the interval lies above zero and the observed gain is positive
The data are inconclusive: zero is plausible, but so are gains up to 4.5, so no effect is not shown

rubric: The CI includes 0 (consistent with p > 0.05) but also meaningful positive gains, so failing to reject is not evidence of no effect.
Equating non-significance with no effect is the key misconception.

items.prompt: An analyst checks an A/B test's p-value every morning and stops the test the first time p < 0.05. Why does this procedure produce more false positives than the nominal 5%?

options.label: Daily looks lower the test's power, and low power mechanically raises the chance of a false positive
Stopping early biases the sample toward users who are more active, which makes the two groups non-comparable
Each look is another chance for the statistic to cross the threshold by luck, so the overall Type I rate exceeds 5%
The p-value shrinks steadily as data accumulate even when the null is true, so later looks almost always appear significant

rubric: Repeated testing gives multiple chances for a chance crossing, inflating the familywise Type I error.
Under a true null the p-value does not drift toward zero; it wanders. Low power affects Type II, not Type I, error.

items.prompt: Blood pressure is measured on the same 30 patients before and after a drug, but the analyst runs a two-sample t-test as if the groups were independent. Which is the main consequence?

options.label: The test ignores the strong within-patient correlation, so the standard error is too large and power drops
The t statistic becomes invalid because paired data cannot follow a t distribution under the null
The Type I error rate rises sharply because the two samples share the same patients
The degrees of freedom are halved, so the critical value moves and the test becomes anti-conservative

rubric: Patient-to-patient variation stays in the error term when pairing is ignored, which inflates the SE and costs power.
The test is usually conservative here, not anti-conservative; the t distribution is still fine for the paired differences.

items.prompt: A chi-square test of independence is run on a 4x5 table in which 12 of the 20 cells have expected counts below 2. What is the most precise problem?

options.label: The observed counts must be at least 5 in every cell, otherwise the null hypothesis can never be rejected at any level
The chi-square approximation to the null distribution is unreliable, so the p-value cannot be trusted
The statistic is computed incorrectly whenever expected counts are small, so the value itself is wrong and must be recalculated
The degrees of freedom must be reduced by one for each sparse cell, so the reported p-value is too small

rubric: The statistic is computable, but its null distribution is only approximately chi-square when expected counts are large enough.
The rule of thumb concerns expected counts, not observed counts, and degrees of freedom are not reduced per cell.

items.prompt: A team runs 20 independent tests on unrelated metrics, all with true null hypotheses, at alpha = 0.05. One test gives p = 0.03 and is reported as a discovery. What does the analysis of this situation show?

options.label: The p = 0.03 value is below 0.05, so the discovery has a 3% chance of being a false positive
The expected number of false positives is exactly one, so that single hit is almost certainly the false one
The result is trustworthy because the tests were independent, which prevents any inflation of error
Under these conditions the chance of at least one p < 0.05 is about 64%, so a lone hit is unremarkable

rubric: The chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95^20, about 0.64, so one hit is expected by chance.
Independence does not remove the multiplicity problem, and p is not the probability that the finding is false.

items.prompt: A website test with 2,000,000 users per arm finds that a redesign reduces page-load time by 0.01 seconds, with p = 0.000001. What explains the tiny p-value?

options.label: A p-value this small shows the null is false by a wide margin, which means the effect is large
The sampling variability is so low that the test must be detecting a practically important change
The huge sample makes the standard error tiny, so even a trivial difference is statistically detectable
The test is flawed because p-values below 0.001 can only occur when the data violate the assumptions

rubric: The p-value reflects effect size relative to the standard error, which shrinks with n; it does not measure importance.
Equating a small p with a large effect is the targeted misconception.

items.prompt: Which situations make the p-value from a one-sample t-test on the mean unreliable? Select all that apply.

options.label: n = 30, roughly symmetric data with a few moderate tails
n = 8, strongly right-skewed data with one extreme outlier
n = 12 readings taken repeatedly from only 4 people, treated as independent
n = 400, mildly right-skewed data with no extreme outliers

rubric: Tiny skewed samples with outliers undermine the normal approximation, and repeated measures break independence.
With moderate or large n and mild skew or symmetry, the central limit theorem keeps the t-test adequate.

items.prompt: A product team randomises each page session to the old or new checkout and compares conversion with a two-proportion z-test over 40,000 sessions, getting p = 0.01. Later they learn that many users contributed several sessions, sometimes landing in both arms. What is the best diagnosis of the analysis?

options.label: The z-test cannot be used for conversion data, so a t-test on session counts should have been used instead
The test is fine because randomisation guarantees valid p-values regardless of how units are defined
Users appearing in both arms makes the test conservative, so the true p-value is even smaller than 0.01
Sessions from one user are correlated, so the independence assumption fails and the standard error is understated

rubric: The randomisation unit differs from the analysis unit, so correlated sessions inflate the effective sample size and understate the SE.
Randomisation validates the test only when the analysis respects the unit that was randomised.

items.prompt: A lab screens 5,000 genes for a link to a disease. Follow-up validation is cheap, and the team accepts that about 5% of flagged genes may be false leads, but wants to miss few real ones. Which approach best meets these criteria?

options.label: Bonferroni correction at 0.05/5000, because it gives the strictest protection against any single false lead among all genes
No correction at 0.05 per gene, because cheap validation will filter out the false leads anyway and misses nothing
Benjamini-Hochberg control of the FDR at 5%, because it keeps more power while bounding the share of false leads
A single combined test across all genes, because testing genes one at a time wastes information shared between them

rubric: The stated tolerance is for a proportion of false leads, which is exactly what FDR control targets while retaining power.
Bonferroni controls familywise error and sacrifices power; uncorrected testing would flood validation with false leads.

items.prompt: A report states: "p = 0.04, so there is a 96% probability that the new teaching method works." Which critique is the most accurate?

options.label: It is correct provided the study was randomised and the sample was large enough to give adequate power
It is wrong because p = 0.04 means only a 4% chance the method works, so it is 96% likely to fail and be useless
It is wrong because the p-value is the chance of data this extreme if the null were true, not the chance the method works
It is wrong because a p-value near 0.05 is too borderline to support any statement about probability, even about the data under the null

rubric: The p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H0), not a posterior probability of either hypothesis.
The 'inverse' reading is the same fallacy, and p-values do make a statement about data under the null.

items.prompt: Two groups of 15 have response times with heavy right skew and two extreme outliers. The goal is to judge whether one group tends to respond slower, and robustness to outliers matters most. Which test best fits these criteria?

options.label: Pooled two-sample t-test, because equal group sizes make it robust to any distribution shape or outliers
Z-test on the means, because variances can be treated as known with 15 per group
Paired t-test, because the groups are the same size and it reduces variance
Mann-Whitney U test, because it uses ranks and so is not driven by the outliers

rubric: Rank-based tests are resistant to outliers and don't require normality, matching the stated priority.
Equal n doesn't rescue the t-test with extreme outliers at n = 15; pairing and known variance don't apply.

items.prompt: A test of a new feature pre-registered a two-sided test. After seeing the treatment mean was higher, the analyst switches to a one-sided test, moving p from 0.07 to 0.035 and declaring significance. How should this be judged?

options.label: Invalid, because choosing the tail after seeing the data effectively doubles the false positive rate
Acceptable, because halving the p-value is a standard adjustment once the sign of the effect is known
Invalid, because one-sided tests are never permitted in product experiments, whatever the justification
Acceptable, because the data show which direction the effect goes, so a one-sided test is more efficient

rubric: Selecting the tail from the observed direction means either tail could have been chosen, so the real alpha is about 10%, not 5%.
One-sided tests are legitimate when prespecified on substantive grounds, but not as a post-hoc rescue.

items.prompt: A manager will ship a change only if the true lift exceeds a minimum worthwhile 2 percentage points. The test gives p = 0.01 and a 95% CI for lift of 0.3 to 1.5 points. Which reporting best serves the decision criterion?

options.label: Report that the test failed, because the CI includes values well below the 2-point threshold and so the lift is not real
Report 'significant, p = 0.01' alone, since it shows the lift is nonzero and so worth shipping
Report the point estimate of about 0.9 only, since intervals add confusion without changing decisions
Show the CI beside the threshold: the lift is real but probably too small to meet the criterion

rubric: The whole CI lies under 2 points, so the effect is probably real but not worth shipping by the stated criterion.
A small p shows only nonzero effect; calling it a failure or dropping the interval ignores the threshold question.

items.prompt: A team wants an A/B test whose reported p-value keeps its stated meaning and whose conclusion is hard to bend after the fact. Which practices best meet that goal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Use a sequential design with alpha spending if interim looks are required
Test fifteen metrics and highlight whichever is most significant
Run until p < 0.05 appears, then freeze the result
Pre-register one primary metric, the test, and the sample size before launching
Remove users who didn't engage after seeing which arm they fell in

rubric: Pre-specification and properly corrected sequential designs preserve the error rate.
Optional stopping, post-randomisation exclusions and cherry-picking among metrics all inflate false positives or bias the estimate.

items.prompt: A first trial of a drug finds a mean improvement of 4.1 points (p = 0.049, 95% CI 0.0 to 8.2). A larger replication finds 2.0 points (p = 0.20, 95% CI -1.1 to 5.1). A colleague says the first result was a fluke and the drug has been shown not to work. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Disagree: the intervals overlap and both allow a modest benefit, so the evidence is inconclusive and pooling is informative
Agree: the replication was larger and non-significant, so it refutes the first result and shows the drug has no effect at all
Disagree: the first trial had p below 0.05, so the replication must have been underpowered and its result can be ignored
Partly agree: a true effect would have replicated at p < 0.05, so the first result was probably a chance finding or error

rubric: Both estimates are positive with wide overlapping CIs; non-significance is not evidence of no effect, and pooling uses all the data.
Treating significance as a replication criterion, or assuming fraud, misreads sampling variability near the threshold.

items.prompt: An analyst checks an A/B test every day and stops as soon as p < 0.05, otherwise continuing up to 30 days. The team treats the nominal 5% as the false-positive rate of this procedure. Which evaluation is best?

options.label: The false-positive rate falls below 5%, because stopping early means fewer observations that could add noise.
The false-positive rate is unaffected, because a p-value under 0.05 is valid whenever the data show a clear trend.
The false-positive rate exceeds 5%, because repeated looks give the null many chances to cross the threshold.
The false-positive rate stays at 5%, because each daily p-value is individually computed at the 0.05 level.

rubric: Repeated peeking with optional stopping inflates the overall Type I error well above the nominal level.
Distractors treat each look as an isolated valid test, ignoring that the chance of at least one crossing accumulates.

items.prompt: A study ran 20 independent subgroup tests, each at alpha = 0.05 with no adjustment, and one subgroup gave p = 0.03. Which judgement of that result is best?

options.label: It is weak evidence, since about one false positive is expected among 20 tests even if all nulls are true.
It is credible evidence, since that test was run at the 0.05 level and its p-value fell below the stated threshold, so the error rate is controlled.
It is strong evidence after correction, since dividing p by 20 gives 0.0015, far below 0.05, which survives any multiplicity adjustment.
It is worthless, since any subgroup analysis is invalid no matter how many tests were run or how it was planned.

rubric: With 20 tests, roughly one nominal hit is expected under the global null, so the result needs replication or proper adjustment.
Dividing p by 20 reverses the Bonferroni correction (which multiplies p), and dismissing all subgroup work overcorrects.

items.prompt: An experiment with 4 million users finds a conversion lift of 0.02 percentage points with p < 0.001. The smallest lift worth shipping is 0.5 points. Which evaluation is best?

options.label: Disregard the result, because samples this large make every p-value meaningless and uninterpretable.
Ship it, because a p-value this small means the true lift is probably close to 0.5 points.
Ship it, because a p-value below 0.001 shows the lift is large and also reliable enough to act on.
Do not ship; the lift is detectable but far below the 0.5-point threshold.

rubric: Huge samples detect trivial effects; the decision should rest on the effect size and its interval relative to the minimum worthwhile effect.
Distractors confuse a small p-value with a large effect, or wrongly claim large samples invalidate inference.

items.prompt: A trial with 12 patients per arm gives p = 0.21 and a 95% CI for the mean difference of -4 to +14 units. Differences above 3 units are clinically important. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: The treatment is harmful, because the lower bound of the interval is negative and the trial found no significant benefit.
The trial is inconclusive, because the interval includes both no effect and important benefit.
The treatment works, because the positive point estimate is supported despite the p-value, given the small sample size.
The treatments perform the same, because p above 0.05 shows there is no effect and the trial was randomised.

rubric: A wide interval covering zero and important effects means the trial is underpowered and cannot show equivalence or benefit.
Distractors read non-significance as proof of no effect, or over-read one end of the interval or the point estimate.

items.prompt: Two groups are compared on mean response: n = 15 with SD 12, and n = 60 with SD 4. The analyst wants Type I error near 5% without assuming equal variances. Which test is best?

options.label: Welch's t-test, because the larger variance sits in the smaller group and the pooled test would reject too often.
The pooled t-test, because the larger sample dominates and makes the equal-variance assumption harmless.
The Mann-Whitney test, because it compares means without any assumption about the groups' spread.
The paired t-test, because it removes the unequal group sizes by matching observations across groups.

rubric: When the smaller group has the larger variance, the pooled t-test is anti-conservative; Welch corrects the standard error and degrees of freedom.
Mann-Whitney does not test means in general and is sensitive to spread differences; pairing does not apply to independent groups.

items.prompt: A report states: 'p = 0.03, so there is a 97% chance the effect is real.' Which critiques of this statement are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: The p-value would be 0.97 if the effect were real, so the report has simply reversed the figure.
The p-value is computed assuming the null is true, so it is not the probability that the null is false.
The chance an effect is real depends on prior plausibility and power, which the p-value does not include.
The statement would be valid if the test had been two-sided rather than one-sided with the same data.

rubric: The p-value is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data); converting needs priors and power.
Sidedness does not change what a p-value means, and p is not 1 minus the probability of a real effect.

items.prompt: A team preplanned a two-sided test of a new checkout design. After seeing that the lift was positive, the analyst reports a one-sided p = 0.04 (the two-sided p is 0.08) and calls it significant at 0.05. Which evaluation is best?

options.label: Invalid, because a one-sided test can never be used for checkout designs, since a lift in either direction is always possible.
Acceptable, because both p-values come from the same data, so the analyst may report whichever one is more convenient.
Acceptable, because the observed lift was positive, and a one-sided test is more powerful for detecting an effect in that direction.
Invalid, because picking the direction after seeing the data halves p unfairly; the preplanned two-sided p = 0.08 stands.

rubric: Sidedness must be fixed before seeing the data; picking it afterward effectively doubles the allowed false-positive rate in the observed direction.
Distractors treat the choice as a convenience or ban one-sided tests entirely, whereas they are valid when prespecified with justification.

items.prompt: You must plan an A/B test to detect a conversion lift from 10% to 12% with 80% power at alpha = 0.05. Which plan best meets these constraints?

options.label: Use the observed lift from a small pilot as the target effect, since it is the best available estimate of the true effect size.
Use 1,000 users per arm, since that is a conventional size that gives adequate power for typical conversion tests.
Check results daily and stop at the first day p drops below 0.05, then record the sample size reached as the plan.
Run a power calculation for the 2-point minimum effect, fix the sample size in advance, and analyze once at that size.

rubric: Power analysis based on the minimum effect of interest and a fixed sample size meets both the power and error-rate constraints.
Stopping on significance inflates error, pilot effects are noisy and often inflated, and a fixed convention ignores the effect size.

items.prompt: Stakeholders want weekly looks at a 6-week experiment, with the option to stop early for efficacy, while the overall false-positive rate stays at 5%. Which design meets these constraints?

options.label: Test at 0.05 each week but require significance in two consecutive weeks, which keeps the overall rate at exactly 5%.
A group sequential design with an alpha-spending function such as O'Brien-Fleming, with stricter early thresholds.
Test at 0.05 at each weekly look and stop at the first significant result, since each look is a valid separate test.
Average the six weekly p-values and compare the mean to 0.05, stopping whenever the running mean falls below it.

rubric: Alpha-spending group sequential designs allocate the total 5% across planned looks, allowing early stopping with valid error control.
The other plans lack a derived error guarantee; ad hoc rules and averaged p-values do not give the stated overall 5% rate.

items.prompt: Before-and-after scores come from the same 15 patients; the within-patient differences are strongly skewed with one outlier. You need an analysis that respects the pairing and does not assume normal differences. Which meets both?

options.label: A chi-square test on before and after scores binned into categories, which needs no distribution assumption.
An unpaired Welch t-test, which handles unequal variances and is robust to skew in small samples.
A Mann-Whitney U test that compares the before scores with the after scores as two separate groups.
A sign-flip permutation test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank test) applied to the within-patient differences.

rubric: Permuting signs of paired differences keeps the pairing and needs no normality assumption.
Mann-Whitney and Welch treat the samples as independent, and binned chi-square also ignores pairing and discards information.

items.prompt: A school randomizes 20 classrooms (10 per arm, about 25 students each) to a new teaching method and records each student's score. Which analysis best respects the design?

options.label: A mixed model with a classroom random effect, or a t-test on the 20 classroom means, since students in a class are correlated.
A chi-square test of students above versus below the overall median, which avoids the clustering problem by using only counts and so ignores class membership.
A t-test on all 500 students, because pooling gives the most power and each student is treated as a separate, independent observation.
A paired t-test of students matched across arms by seat position, which is assumed to account for the classroom effects in the design.

rubric: Randomization was at classroom level, so the effective sample is closer to 20 clusters; the analysis must account for within-class correlation.
A student-level t-test gives overstated precision; matching by seat or dichotomizing does not remove clustering.

items.prompt: A generic drug must be shown to be no worse than the standard drug by more than 3 percentage points in response rate. Which analysis plan meets this requirement?

options.label: Run a two-sided test of equal rates at alpha 0.05 and conclude non-inferiority if the observed difference is within 3 points of zero.
Prespecify the 3-point margin, test the null that the generic is worse by 3 or more, and require the CI lower bound to exceed -3.
Choose the margin after seeing the data, based on the width of the confidence interval, so that the interval sits inside it comfortably.
Run a two-sided test of equal rates with a large sample and conclude non-inferiority whenever the p-value is above 0.05.

rubric: Non-inferiority requires a prespecified margin and a one-sided null of inferiority, judged against the CI bound.
Non-significance in a difference test is not evidence of non-inferiority, and a post hoc margin invalidates the claim.

items.prompt: A team wants an A/B test to be genuinely confirmatory. Which elements should the preregistered plan fix before data collection? Select all that apply.

options.label: Whichever secondary metric turns out most significant, which will be named the primary afterward.
The choice of one-sided or two-sided testing, made once the direction of the lift is visible.
The sample size or stopping rule, so the number of looks at the data is known.
The primary metric, the direction of the hypothesis, and the significance level.
The statistical test and the rules for excluding observations, decided before outcomes are seen.

rubric: Confirmatory inference requires fixing hypothesis, error rate, stopping rule, test and exclusions in advance to avoid researcher degrees of freedom.
Naming the primary metric or sidedness after seeing results makes the p-value uninterpretable.

items.prompt: An experiment measures weekly spend per user; variance is large and the test is underpowered. Each user's spend in the 4 pre-experiment weeks, recorded before randomization, correlates r = 0.8 with the outcome. Which analysis best raises power without adding bias?

options.label: Adjust for post-randomization engagement, which correlates strongly with spend and soaks up variance.
Adjust for pre-experiment spend as a covariate (ANCOVA or CUPED), which removes variance it explains.
Switch to a one-sided test after observing the direction of the lift, which gives more power cheaply.
Drop users whose spend is far from the average after seeing outcomes, which shrinks variance.

rubric: A pre-randomization covariate strongly correlated with the outcome reduces variance without biasing the treatment estimate.
Post-treatment covariates can absorb part of the effect, and outcome-based exclusions or post hoc sidedness invalidate inference.
